Apple has submitted its proposals regarding the fees charged on transactions outside the App Store system in the Epic Games lawsuit. Here are the relevant details.

Apple Submits Out-of-App Store Commission Proposal

After multiple requests to stay the district court proceedings—which will determine whether and how Apple can charge fees on transactions outside of its IAP system in the App Store—Apple has now submitted its proposals, outlining the suggested fee structure.

Apple's submission comes right after the Supreme Court denied Apple's request to stay the lower court proceedings. Apple had hoped to pause the proceedings while the Supreme Court reviewed whether it would be held in contempt for charging a 27% commission on transactions outside the App Store. Previously, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers had issued an injunction requiring Apple to allow developers to direct users to other purchasing methods.

Apple argued in the lower court, and subsequently in the Supreme Court, that the court's decision could affect the outcome of the fee determination process, so the proceedings should be stayed until the court issued its ruling. However, the Supreme Court denied Apple's request, allowing the lower court proceedings to continue while the review is underway.

Therefore, Apple has now submitted its proposals, suggesting the following fees:

15% for standard apps (which are subject to the 30% In-App Purchase ("IAP") commission);

Apple stated, "The factual and expert evidence regarding these proposed commission rates has also been submitted simultaneously." The company added:

Apple added that its "proposed out-of-link commissions can also be compared to the commissions of other competing app stores," including Google Play, Samsung Galaxy Store, and Amazon's Android App Marketplace.

The company also noted, "The Google Play Store's standard out-of-link fee structure is: standard rate 20%, program rate 15%, subscription rate 10%—rates to which Epic has also agreed."

Apple stated that it still believes the fee determination process should be stayed pending the outcome of the case before the Supreme Court, and added that the submission of this proposal is only to comply with Judge Gonzalez Rogers's instructions.

The company also pointed out that the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has overturned the district court's blanket injunction on out-of-link transaction commissions, and stated that the relevant commissions would only pose a problem if they effectively constituted a constructive ban.

Following the submission of the proposals, Epic can now respond, and Apple is expected to submit its brief to the Supreme Court before September 14.
